paragraph_ledger.text:
The background prediction is obtained from the simulated samples introduced in Section~\ref{sec:background_samples}, with the dominant $W$+jets and top-quark contributions normalised to data in control regions (CRs).
This chapter describes these constraints, the treatment of the small fake-$\tau$ contribution, and the validation of the prediction in regions outside the SRs.
The object definitions and SR selections follow Chapters~\ref{chapter:object_reconstruction} and~\ref{chapter:event_selection}.

sentence_units.text: The background prediction is obtained from the simulated samples introduced in Section~\ref{sec:background_samples}, with the dominant $W$+jets and top-quark contributions normalised to data in control regions (CRs).
This chapter describes these constraints, the treatment of the small fake-$\tau$ contribution, and the validation of the prediction in regions outside the SRs.
The object definitions and SR selections follow Chapters~\ref{chapter:object_reconstruction} and~\ref{chapter:event_selection}.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The CRs provide data samples enriched in the backgrounds to be normalised, with little signal contamination.
Four CRs are used: $\CRW$-$\Res$ and $\CRW$-$\NonRes$ constrain $W$+jets, while $\CRTop$-$\Res$ and $\CRTop$-$\NonRes$ constrain top-quark production.
Each region contributes its total event count to a simultaneous fit.
The fitted normalisation factors, $\lambda_W^{\Res}$, $\lambda_W^{\NonRes}$, $\lambda_t^{\Res}$ and $\lambda_t^{\NonRes}$, multiply the corresponding simulated yields in the CRs, SRs and validation regions (VRs).
The same top-quark factor is applied to $\ttbar$ and single-top production within each topology.
Separate factors for the resonant and non-resonant categories allow the normalisation to differ between the high- and low-jet-$\pT$ selections.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The extrapolation from a CR to an SR is supplied by simulation: the fit fixes the background rate in the CR, while the simulated ratio of SR to CR yields determines the rate transferred to the SR.
The $W$+jets extrapolation therefore depends on the description of the lepton flavour and jet flavour, and the top-quark extrapolation also depends on the acceptance of the additional lepton and the relaxed CR requirements.
The relevant uncertainties are described in Chapter~\ref{chapter:systematics_uncertainties}.
Diboson and $Z$+jets production, together with the other small contributions, retain their simulated nominal yields and are allowed to vary within their assigned uncertainties in the fit.
The fitted uncertainty parameters are propagated to the SRs and VRs together with the normalisation factors.
The multijet suppression is already described in Section~\ref{subsec:ch7_multijet} and Appendix~\ref{App:QCD_bkg_study}.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The VRs test these extrapolations without contributing event counts to the background-only fit.
Their object multiplicities are summarised in Table~\ref{tab:ch8_region_roles}.
In particular, $\VRb$ tests the change from a $b$-jet veto to one tagged jet, and $\VRTop$ tests the prediction for a hadronic $\tau$ with no selected light lepton.
The zero-$b$-jet regions containing a $\tau$ are the $\bVetoSR$ regions defined in Section~\ref{sec:ch7_sr0b}.
The likelihood construction and the final fitted normalisation factors are reserved for Chapter~\ref{chapter:results}.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The $\CRW$ regions select $W\to\ell\nu$ events by replacing the $\tau$ in the corresponding $\bVetoSR$ selection with an electron or muon.
The $b$-jet veto suppresses top-quark production and provides a larger $W$+jets sample than a tagged selection.
Exactly one signal electron or muon and no selected $\tau$ are required.
The signal-lepton requirements are those in Chapter~\ref{chapter:object_reconstruction}.
Single-lepton triggers are used, as listed in Section~\ref{sec:analysis_triggers}.
This choice avoids the different response of the calorimeter-based $\met$ trigger to electrons and muons, since the trigger-level missing momentum does not include the muon momentum.

The relevant decays include $\ttbar\to b\tau\nu\,\bar b\ell\nu$ and $Wt\to b\tau\nu\,\ell\nu$.
The additional lepton selects the second leptonic $W$ decay and separates these regions from the lepton-vetoed SRs.
Requiring at least one tagged $b$ jet further suppresses $W$+jets production.
Inclusive $\ttbar$ and single-top samples are used.
Within the $\ttbar$ and $Wt$ samples, the large-$\met$ selection favours decays in which both $W$ bosons decay leptonically.
This explains the dominant modes identified above without restricting the prediction to those modes.
The top-quark purity is approximately $90\%$ after the full CR selections.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The selected SM background is dominated by events containing a genuine hadronically decaying $\tau$, so the fake-$\tau$ contribution is small.
As discussed in Section~\ref{sec:ch7_sr1b}, its principal source at large $\met$ is $Z\to\nu\nu$+jets, where a jet passes the $\tau$ identification.
This contribution is at most about $10\%$ of the background in the SRs considered in the fake-rate study and is much smaller in the one-$b$-jet SRs.
It is retained in the prediction rather than set to zero.
The nominal yield is taken from simulation, and a dedicated $Z\to\ell\ell$ study determines an uncertainty for the modelling of jets misidentified as $\tau$ candidates.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The $Z$ validation region (ZVR) selects a visible $Z$ decay together with a $\tau$ candidate to test the simulated fake rate in a sample enriched in $Z$+jets.
Two signal electrons or two signal muons are required, with $75<m_{\ell\ell}<105~\GeV$, together with exactly one $\tau$ candidate and a $b$-jet veto.
The jet multiplicity satisfies $1\leq N_j\leq3$ and $\pT^\tau>100~\GeV$.
Both lepton channels are used to increase the statistical precision.
The muon channel uses the $\met$ trigger, whereas the electron channel uses a single-electron trigger.

paragraph_ledger.text:
A total of 116 data events pass the ZVR selection, and the simulated $Z$+jets purity is approximately $90\%$.
Figure~\ref{fig:ch8_zvr_pt} shows the $\pT^\tau$ distribution with its threshold removed.
The simulation overestimates the yield at high $\pT^\tau$.
Differences of up to $60\%$ are observed in the overall yields in the validation comparisons.
This comparison alone is sensitive to both the fake rate and the production kinematics of $Z$+jets.
The RNN-score distributions in Figure~\ref{fig:ch8_zvr_rnn} provide a further check using looser $\tau$ identification and a relaxed transverse-mass requirement.
They compare samples with $\pT^\tau>20~\GeV$ and $\pT^\tau>100~\GeV$.
The better agreement at low RNN scores indicates that the discrepancy is mainly connected to the probability for a jet to pass the $\tau$ identification.

The tagged jet replaces the leading untagged jet in the topology and invariant-mass selections.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The excess in $\VRb$-$\NonRes$ remains a deviation of about $2\sigma$ after the background-only fit and the assigned uncertainties are included.
Its origin is examined through the cutflow, nearby $\met$ selections and the properties of the selected data events.
The pre-fit ratio stays close to unity until the $\met>400~\GeV$ requirement is imposed.
A finer-binned comparison locates much of the excess in $425<\met<450~\GeV$, as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:ch8_vrw_met_study}.
Changing the $\met$ threshold to $300~\GeV$ or $500~\GeV$ reduces the discrepancy in the statistical-only checks to $1.8\sigma$ and $1.5\sigma$, respectively.
This behaviour indicates a local excess rather than a persistent offset throughout the high-$\met$ tail.

paragraph_ledger.text:
Within $425<\met<450~\GeV$, the excess is concentrated in the $300<\pT^\ell<400~\GeV$ bin, above the $200~\GeV$ lepton threshold.

paragraph_ledger.text:
The additional $1\tau0\ell1b$ regions test the background with the same object multiplicities as $\SR$ in adjacent mass intervals.
They provide a direct check of the one-$b$-jet, hadronic-$\tau$ prediction following the excess in the light-lepton validation sample.
The resonant region requires $400<m_{b\tau}<800~\GeV$, and the non-resonant region requires $500<\mT<600~\GeV$.
These upper bounds keep the regions separate from the corresponding SRs.
Further reductions in $\pT^\tau$, $\met$ and $\mT$ increase the event yields, as summarised in Table~\ref{tab:ch8_tau1b_vr}.
All other requirements follow the corresponding $\SR$ selections.

paragraph_ledger.text:
Signal contamination is evaluated before examining the data, using the same benchmarks as in Section~\ref{subsec:ch8_vrtop}.
The estimated contributions are about $2\%$ and $7\%$ in the resonant and non-resonant regions, respectively.
The CR fit then predicts $25.4\pm1.5$ and $8.0\pm1.7$ background events, compared with 24 and 9 observed events.
The agreement supports the transfer of the background normalisation to the $1\tau0\ell1b$ final state in these lower-mass intervals.
No additional uncertainty for the changed $m_{b\tau}$ or $\mT$ selections is included in this supplementary study, so its agreement is a cross-check rather than a separate determination of the uncertainty in the high-mass SR prediction.
